title: URL Shortener: Complete Architecture
description: Design a scalable URL shortener like bit.ly with caching, analytics, and global distribution.

data.text: Design a URL shortening service similar to bit.ly or TinyURL. Users paste long URLs and receive short, shareable links (e.g., https://bit.ly/3xK9mP). The system must handle 500 million redirects per day, ensure sub-50ms P99 redirect latency at the edge, support custom aliases, analytics tracking per click, link expiration, and be available in multiple geographic regions with 99.99% uptime.

terms.definition: Encoding scheme using [A-Z, a-z, 0-9] to generate compact short codes (6 chars = 56 billion possibilities).
Application checks cache first; on miss, loads from DB and populates cache for future reads.
Redirect responses cached at geographically distributed edge nodes to serve users with minimal latency.
Distribution strategy that minimises key remapping when nodes are added or removed.
Analytics writes buffered in Redis, flushed asynchronously to the database to avoid write amplification.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Shorten any valid URL to a 6-character Base62 code (e.g., https://sho.rt/aB3xKz)
Support custom vanity aliases (e.g., /product-launch) with uniqueness validation
Redirect short URL → original URL with HTTP 301 (permanent) or 302 (trackable)
Track analytics: click count, referrer, user-agent, country, timestamp per click
Set optional expiration (TTL) on links; expired links return 410 Gone
Bulk URL creation via CSV upload for enterprise tier
QR code generation for each short link
Rate limiting: 100 creates/hour for free tier, unlimited for paid

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: 500 million redirects/day (~5,800 req/s avg, ~50,000 req/s peak)
Sub-50ms P99 redirect latency from CDN edge cache
99.99% availability for redirect endpoints (≤52 min downtime/year)
Write path: 10 million new URLs/day (~115 creates/s)
Analytics: at-least-once delivery, eventual consistency acceptable (lag ≤30s)
Horizontal scaling with no single point of failure
Cross-region active-active replication for global low latency

data.text: The system separates the high-throughput read path (redirects) from the low-throughput write path (URL creation) and the async analytics pipeline. CDN edge caching absorbs the majority of redirect traffic before it ever reaches origin servers.

rows: Base62 short code or custom alias

items.question: Why Base62 over MD5/SHA hashing?
items.answer: Hashing creates collision risk requiring retries and longer codes. Base62 with a distributed counter guarantees uniqueness with predictable 6-character output. Snowflake IDs provide globally unique 64-bit integers that encode cleanly to Base62.

items.question: 301 (Permanent) vs 302 (Temporary) redirect?
items.answer: 301 lets browsers cache the redirect permanently, reducing server load — but click analytics are lost since the browser never hits your server again. 302 forces the browser to always hit your server, enabling accurate click tracking at the cost of higher origin traffic. Choose based on analytics requirements.

items.question: How to handle hot links (viral URLs)?
items.answer: A small % of URLs receive 80%+ of traffic. Use a two-tier cache: in-process L1 cache (LRU, 10k entries) for truly hot links, and Redis L2 for the long tail. CDN edge caching absorbs the remaining burst before it reaches origin.

items.question: How to prevent abuse and malicious URLs?
items.answer: Integrate Google Safe Browsing API to scan destination URLs at creation time. Use Bloom filters to quickly detect known-bad domains. Apply rate limiting per user/IP with token bucket algorithm backed by Redis.

items.question: How to scale the write path for 10M URLs/day?
items.answer: The write path is 100x lighter than reads. Two ASP.NET Core instances behind a load balancer handle 115 creates/second easily. Shard the distributed ID generator (Zookeeper-assigned ranges) to eliminate ID generation as a bottleneck.

data.title: Interview Tip: Start with scale numbers
data.text: In interviews, always start by deriving scale: 500M redirects/day ÷ 86,400s = ~5,800 req/s average. With a 10:1 peak-to-average ratio, plan for 58,000 req/s peak. This drives every architectural decision that follows.

terms.term: Assume 80% of traffic hits 20% of URLs (Pareto)

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Read-to-write ratio is ~50:1; optimise the redirect path relentlessly with multi-tier caching
Base62 encoding of distributed Snowflake IDs gives unique, compact, collision-free codes
Separate the fast redirect path (sync) from analytics (async Kafka pipeline)
301 reduces server load; 302 enables per-click tracking — choose based on requirements
CDN edge caching is the single biggest lever for latency and origin capacity
data.takeaway: A URL shortener is deceptively simple at small scale but requires careful cache hierarchy, async analytics separation, and distributed ID generation to handle billions of daily redirects reliably.
